subject: Business
specVersion: Issue 2 (July 2022) as shown on the specification PDF opened; first teaching 2017, first assessment 2019
statusNote: Qualification matched to the school's lesson content: the Year 10 and Year 11 lesson files cite Edexcel GCSE Business (1BS0) and use the 1BS0 unit titles (Theme 1 Investigating small business, 1.1 to 1.3; Theme 2 Building a business, 2.1), so 1BS0 is documented here. Paper structure, marks, weightings, AOs, Theme 1 and Theme 2 topics and sub-topic content were read from the Pearson 1BS0 specification PDF (read through a page-summarising fetch tool, not a manual page-by-page read). The International GCSE Business 4BS1 structure was also read and is recorded under gaps; the school's Year 11 parent presentation says 'IGCSE Edexcel', so the qualification entered must be CONFIRMED with the board and the exams officer before entries. Year allocation (Theme 1 in Year 10, Theme 2 in Year 11) is a recommended sequence, not a board requirement.

sources.title: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9-1) Business (2017) qualification page
Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Business 4BS1 specification (PDF), read for comparison only

tiers: None (single tier of entry; no foundation or higher papers)

assessment.title: Investigating small business (1BS0/01)
assessment.format: Three sections (A 35 marks, B 30 marks, C 25 marks); calculations, multiple choice, short answer and extended writing; Sections B and C use a source booklet

assessment.title: Building a business (1BS0/02)
assessment.format: Three sections (A 35 marks, B 30 marks, C 25 marks); calculations, multiple choice, short answer and extended writing; Sections B and C use a source booklet

nonExam: None: assessed entirely by two externally marked written papers. Quantitative skills make up 10% of total marks and are assessed on both papers; calculators allowed, formulae not provided.

aos.desc: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of business concepts and issues
Apply knowledge and understanding to a variety of business contexts
Analyse and evaluate business information and issues to make judgements

units.title: Enterprise and entrepreneurship
points: New business ideas arise from changing technology, changing wants and products becoming obsolete (1.1.1)
Ideas may be wholly original or adapt existing products, services or ideas (1.1.1)
Risk covers business failure, financial loss and lack of security; reward covers profit, success and independence (1.1.2)
Enterprise meets customer needs by producing goods or services (1.1.3)
Businesses add value through convenience, branding, quality, design and a unique selling point (1.1.3)
Entrepreneurs organise resources, make decisions and take risks (1.1.3)

units.title: Spotting a business opportunity
points: Customers typically need price, quality, choice and convenience; meeting needs supports sales and survival (1.2.1)
Market research finds needs and gaps in the market and reduces risk (1.2.2)
Primary methods (surveys, questionnaires, focus groups, observation) versus secondary sources (internet, market and government reports) (1.2.2)
Qualitative and quantitative data; reliability of research findings (1.2.2)
Segmentation by location, demographics, lifestyle, income and age; market mapping shows gaps and competitors (1.2.3)
Assessing competitors on price, quality, location, range and service (1.2.4)

units.title: Putting a business idea into practice
points: Aims are broad goals; objectives are specific, measurable targets; both may be financial or non-financial (1.3.1)
Revenue, fixed and variable costs, total costs, profit and loss, interest, break-even and margin of safety (1.3.2)
Calculations: revenue = price x quantity; total costs = fixed + variable; break-even units; margin of safety (1.3.2)
Interpret break-even diagrams for changes in costs, revenue and profit (1.3.2)
Cash and profit differ; cash-flow forecasts show inflows, outflows, net cash flow and balances (1.3.3)
Short-term finance: overdraft, trade credit. Long-term: savings, venture capital, share capital, loans, retained profit, crowdfunding (1.3.4)

units.title: Making the business effective
points: Limited and unlimited liability and what each means for owners (1.4.1)
Sole trader, partnership, private limited company and franchise: advantages and disadvantages (1.4.1)
Location depends on proximity to market, labour, materials and competitors, and on e-commerce (1.4.2)
The marketing mix of price, product, promotion and place must work together (1.4.3)
Technology such as e-commerce and digital communication affects the mix (1.4.3)
A business plan covers idea, aims, target market, forecasts, finance, location and mix; it reduces risk and helps secure finance (1.4.4)

units.title: Understanding external influences on business
points: Stakeholders include shareholders, employees, customers, managers, suppliers, community, pressure groups and government (1.5.1)
Stakeholder interests can conflict; business activity and stakeholders affect each other (1.5.1)
Technology: e-commerce, social media, digital communication and payment systems affect sales, costs and marketing (1.5.2)
Consumer law and employment law; compliance costs and consequences of breaking the law (1.5.3)
Economic climate: unemployment, consumer income, inflation, interest rates, taxation and exchange rates (1.5.4)
Businesses respond to changes in external influences by adapting products, prices or operations (1.5.5)

units.title: Growing the business
points: Organic growth through new products or new markets; external growth through mergers and takeovers (2.1.1)
Growing businesses may become public limited companies and float on the stock market (2.1.1)
Finance for growth: retained profit and asset sales (internal); loans and share capital (external) (2.1.1)
Aims and objectives change with market conditions, technology, performance and legislation (2.1.2)
Imports, exports, multinationals, tariffs and trade blocs affect international business (2.1.3)
Competing internationally via the internet, e-commerce and the marketing mix (2.1.3)
Ethical and environmental considerations can involve trade-offs with profit; pressure groups can affect the mix (2.1.4)

units.title: Making marketing decisions
points: Product: design mix of function, aesthetics and cost; product life cycle and extension strategies; differentiation (2.2.1)
Price: pricing strategies and influences such as competition, segments, technology and life cycle (2.2.2)
Promotion: advertising, sponsorship, trials, offers, branding and technology-based promotion (2.2.3)
Place: retailers, e-tailers and choosing a distribution method for the target market (2.2.4)
Elements of the mix influence each other and build competitive advantage when integrated (2.2.5)

units.title: Making operational decisions
points: Production types: job, batch and flow, and their effect on productivity, costs and pricing (2.3.1)
Technology in production: balancing cost, productivity, quality and flexibility (2.3.1)
Stock management, interpreting stock-level graphs and just-in-time (JIT) control (2.3.2)
Procurement: supplier choice by quality, delivery, availability, cost and trust; effects of logistics (2.3.2)
Quality control and quality assurance help control costs and gain advantage (2.3.3)
The sales process: product knowledge, speed, engagement, feedback and after-sales service (2.3.4)

units.title: Making financial decisions
points: Gross profit = sales revenue minus cost of sales; net profit = gross profit minus expenses and interest (2.4.1)
Gross and net profit margins as percentages of sales revenue (2.4.1)
Average rate of return = average annual profit divided by cost of investment, as a percentage (2.4.1)
Formulae are not given in the exam and must be learned (2.4.1)
Use quantitative data (graphs, financial and market data) to support decisions (2.4.2)
Judge the uses and limitations of financial information (2.4.2)

units.title: Making human resource decisions
points: Hierarchical and flat structures; centralised and decentralised decision-making (2.5.1)
Communication effects and barriers; part-time, full-time, flexible, temporary and freelance working (2.5.1)
Job roles, job description, person specification, application form, CV; internal and external recruitment (2.5.2)
Training methods, performance reviews and the link to motivation and retention (2.5.3)
Financial motivation: pay, bonuses, commission, promotion, fringe benefits (2.5.4)
Non-financial motivation: job rotation, job enrichment, autonomy (2.5.4)

commandWords.meaning: Give the meaning of a term from the specification
Give a one-sentence answer drawn from the context
Use maths on given data; show working
Give two linked points about a concept in context
Give a statement with two expansion points (no context needed)
Extended answer exploring a concept in the context given
Extended answer exploring an issue; context optional
Use the information given to recommend one of two options
Use knowledge to reach a supported judgement or conclusion

skills: Business calculations: revenue, costs, profit, break-even, margin of safety, profit margins, average rate of return
Cash-flow forecasts: net cash flow, opening and closing balances
Percentages, percentage change and averages (minimum KS3 mathematics)
Reading graphs, charts, break-even diagrams and stock-level graphs
Applying knowledge to a source booklet or case study
Extended writing: analysis, justification and evaluation with a reasoned conclusion

prerequisites.from: KS3 Mathematics: percentages, ratio and averages
KS3 Mathematics: algebraic substitution and graphs
1.1 Risk and reward; 1.3.4 Sources of finance

links.how: Maths provides the methods; Business applies them to profit margins and average rate of return
Break-even and margin of safety use formulae and straight-line graphs; Maths supplies the technique
Promotion and branding use persuasive language; English develops the analysis of purpose and audience
Evaluate questions need a structured argument with a justified conclusion
Geography covers where and why trade and production locate; Business covers the decisions firms make
Sources of finance such as loans and interest can be discussed alongside Islamic principles of lawful trade, kept factual and accurate
Ethical business decisions and social responsibility can be compared with Islamic teaching on fair dealing and charity, taught accurately and separately from the specification

links.topic: E-commerce, digital communication and payment systems
links.how: Computing explains how the technology works; Business assesses its effect on sales, costs and marketing

links.topic: Personal finance, careers and employment rights
links.how: Employment law, recruitment and pay in Business support PSHE work on work and money
Science gives evidence on environmental effects; Business weighs these against cost and profit

contextNote: Specification topics 2.1.4 (ethics, environment and sustainability) require pupils to weigh ethical and environmental considerations against profit; teach the range of business viewpoints accurately and let pupils evaluate. Islamic perspectives in the links are enrichment and are not examined.
gaps: BOARD CONFIRMATION NEEDED: the school's Year 11 parent presentation says 'IGCSE Edexcel' for Business Studies, but the lesson content follows GCSE (9-1) Business 1BS0. Confirm which qualification candidates will be entered for.

For comparison, International GCSE (9-1) Business 4BS1 (Issue 2, February 2026 on the PDF opened): Paper 1 Investigating small businesses (4BS1/01) 1 hour 30 minutes, 80 marks, 50%; Paper 2 Investigating large businesses (4BS1/02) 1 hour 30 minutes, 80 marks, 50%; four compulsory 20-mark questions each; single tier; AO1 27-28%, AO2 38-39%, AO3 22-23%, AO4 11-12%; quantitative skills 10%.

4BS1 sections read at title level only: 1 Business activity and influences on business (1.1 to 1.8), 2 People in business (2.1 to 2.5), 3 Business finance (3.1 to 3.5), 4 Marketing (4.1 to 4.3), 5 Business operations (5.1 to 5.4). Bullet-level 4BS1 content was not read, so units are not mapped to it.
If the entry is 4BS1 the unit list, papers, durations, marks, assessment objectives and sequencing in this file would need replacing; lesson unit titles do not match 4BS1.
The school's lesson files currently cover 1.1, 1.2, the start of 1.3 (Year 10) and 2.1 (Year 11) only; topics 1.3 (cash flow, finance), 1.4, 1.5 and 2.2 to 2.5 are not yet written as lessons.
Sample assessment materials and mark schemes were not opened; command word meanings come from the specification PDF summary.
Spec issue number was taken from the PDF text as read; check Pearson's site for any later issue before entries.
